summary: A tragedy of grief, doubt, disgust, and delay, in which a prince's hatred of his father's murderer is held back by uncertainty, shame, and melancholy.

need-to-breathe.why: Ophelia drowns, pulled under by her sodden garments in Gertrude's report, and Hamlet's last words come as the poison stops his breath, but breath is not dwelt on.

hungry.why: Hamlet's joke that the funeral baked meats coldly furnished the marriage tables is about thrift, not appetite; no one hungers.

thirsty.why: No one lacks drink; the poisoned cup is pledged, not craved.

sleepy.why: The watch keeps sleepless vigil for the Ghost, King Hamlet was poisoned sleeping in his orchard, and Hamlet, restless at sea, cannot sleep and finds the sealed commission.

nauseous.why: No one sickens from food or poison in that way; the poisons kill outright.

dizzy.why: No one reels; the dying fall from poison, not faintness.

fatigued.why: Gertrude remarks during the fencing match that Hamlet is fat and scant of breath, and offers her napkin, but exertion plays no larger part.

pain.why: Laertes and Hamlet are both cut by the envenomed foil, Gertrude and Claudius die of poison, and the Ghost describes being burnt and purged in fires.

disgusted.why: Hamlet rails at the rank sweat of his mother's enseamed bed, at the incestuous sheets, at the unweeded garden of the world, and holds his nose at Yorick's skull.

over-stimulated.why: No sense is overwhelmed; Claudius's cannon are noise, not assault.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Francisco complains that it is bitter cold on the battlements and Hamlet that the air bites shrewdly, but the cold is atmosphere, not trouble.

afraid.why: The sentries and Horatio are harrowed with fear and wonder at the Ghost, Claudius grows afraid of Hamlet's madness, and Hamlet's soliloquy names the dread of something after death.

anxious.why: Hamlet broods on what to do through four acts, Claudius frets that Hamlet's madness is dangerous and ships him off, and Polonius worries over Ophelia's honor.

panic.why: Claudius bolts from the Mousetrap crying for lights, and Gertrude screams for help in the closet scene, bringing Polonius's cry that gets him killed.

sensory-pleasures.why: Claudius keeps wassail with cannon fired at every draught, and Hamlet imagines his mother living in the rank sweat of her bed with Claudius.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Hamlet delights in the players, recites the Pyrrhus speech from memory, and instructs them on acting before staging The Mousetrap.

fun-excitement.why: Hamlet plays cat and mouse with Polonius and Osric, trades riddles with the gravedigger, and the court gathers for the fencing match as sport.

orgasm.why: Gertrude's bed is talked of constantly, but no sexual act occurs.

love-romantic.why: Hamlet's letters to Ophelia, his cruelty to her, and his claim at her grave that he loved her more than forty thousand brothers, with Claudius and Gertrude's hasty marriage, make love central but poisoned.

love-family.why: Hamlet's devotion to his murdered father and torment over his mother, and Laertes' fury at Polonius's death and Ophelia's drowning, drive both revenge plots.

grief.why: Hamlet enters in mourning black for his father, Ophelia loses her reason after Polonius's murder, and Laertes and Hamlet grapple in her grave.

missing-someone.why: Hamlet says he shall not look upon his father's like again, and Ophelia's mad songs circle around a dead old man and a lost lover.

aroused-sexually.why: Hamlet obsesses over his mother's lust for Claudius, the Ghost calls her a seeming-virtuous queen led by lust, and Hamlet taunts Ophelia with country matters.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Horatio is the one man Hamlet trusts and the one he asks to live and tell his story, while Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's false friendship earns them death.

empathy.why: Hamlet marvels that a player can weep for Hecuba and wonders at his own cold heart, and later sees his own cause in Laertes' grief.

compassion.why: Horatio tends Hamlet to the end and would drink the poison with him, and Gertrude speaks gently to the mad Ophelia and strews flowers on her grave.

grateful.why: Hamlet tells Horatio he wears him in his heart's core, and Claudius thanks Rosencrantz and Guildenstern for coming, but gratitude is slight.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern profess eagerness to serve the king, and Horatio serves Hamlet, but no one takes pleasure in helping.

trustful-distrustful.why: Hamlet doubts whether the Ghost is a devil, sees through Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, suspects Ophelia is bait, and Claudius and Polonius spy on everyone, even Laertes in Paris.

depressed.why: Hamlet, alone in a court that has moved on, finds the world weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable, wishes his flesh would melt, and has lost all his mirth.

angry.why: Hamlet rages at his mother in the closet, stabs through the arras, and Laertes storms the palace shouting that he will be revenged most thoroughly for his father.

envious.why: Claudius killed his brother for his crown and queen, and he tells Laertes that Hamlet grew envious hearing a Norman praise Laertes' fencing.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: The Ghost burns that Claudius won his queen, and Hamlet's obsession with his mother's bed has the color of jealousy, but no lover guards a rival here.

jealous-friendship.why: Hamlet's bitterness that his schoolfellows now serve Claudius has a trace of this, but no friendship rank is contested.

hatred.why: Hamlet hates Claudius as a remorseless, treacherous, lecherous, kindless villain, Claudius plots Hamlet's death in England and then with Laertes, and Laertes would cut Hamlet's throat in church.

contempt.why: Hamlet calls Polonius a tedious old fool, Osric a waterfly, Rosencrantz a sponge, and Claudius a king of shreds and patches; scorn is his native tongue.

resentment.why: Hamlet resents that Claudius popped in between the election and his hopes, and Laertes resents Polonius's obscure funeral with no trophy, sword, or hatchment.

proud.why: Hamlet measures himself against Fortinbras's twenty thousand men who find quarrel in a straw when honor is at the stake, and Laertes' honor demands revenge.

amused.why: Hamlet's puns on Polonius and Osric, the gravedigger's riddles about who builds strongest, and the memory of Yorick's jests give the play its laughter.

sense-of-belonging.why: Hamlet feels Denmark a prison and himself a stranger at Claudius's court, while Laertes commands a mob that would crown him king.

lonely.why: Hamlet confides only in Horatio and the audience, Ophelia, abandoned by Hamlet and then orphaned, has no one, and both end alone.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Hamlet judges Claudius a murderer and his mother frail, the priest grudges Ophelia Christian burial, and the play weighs revenge, suicide, and incest as moral questions throughout.

admiration.why: Hamlet calls his father Hyperion and praises Horatio as a man who is not passion's slave, and Ophelia mourns Hamlet as the glass of fashion and the mould of form.

embarrassed.why: Ophelia squirms at Hamlet's bawdy jokes before the whole court at the play, and Polonius is made ridiculous over camels, weasels, and whales.

shame.why: Hamlet calls himself a rogue and peasant slave for failing to act, Gertrude sees black and grained spots in her soul, and Claudius knows his offence is rank and smells to heaven.

guilt.why: Claudius cannot pray because he keeps the crown and queen he killed for, Hamlet repents Polonius's death, and the dying Laertes confesses he is justly killed by his own treachery.

sad.why: Hamlet's loss of father and crown, Ophelia's willow song, and Horatio's good night sweet prince keep sorrow in the air of every act.

happy.why: Claudius is content at his wedding feast, but Hamlet has lost all his mirth and no one else in Elsinore is happy for long.

joyful-euphoric.why: Hamlet is briefly exultant when the Mousetrap catches the king's conscience, calling for music and recorders and taking the Ghost's word for a thousand pound.

effort.why: Hamlet's whole problem is whether to persist in the task the Ghost set him; he chides himself for letting resolution sicken into thought.

focused-in-flow.why: Hamlet is briefly absorbed in coaching the players and writing his dozen lines, but absorption is rare in a play about distraction.

bored.why: Hamlet finds all the uses of this world weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable, a boredom with life that borders on his melancholy.

distracted.why: Hamlet is described as distracted, lets Claudius pass at prayer on a quibble, and his purpose is forever turned awry by thinking; Ophelia goes distracted outright.

impatient.why: The Ghost returns to whet Hamlet's almost blunted purpose, Laertes will not wait but would cut Hamlet's throat in church, and Hamlet reproaches his own delay.

curious.why: Hamlet stages The Mousetrap to test the Ghost's word, Polonius sends Reynaldo to spy on Laertes, and Claudius sets Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to find out Hamlet's secret.

surprised.why: Horatio and the watch are amazed by the Ghost, Hamlet learns from it that his father was murdered, and he finds the sealed order for his own death aboard ship.

awe.why: The Ghost in full armor fills the watch with fear and wonder, and Hamlet tells Horatio there are more things in heaven and earth than his philosophy dreams of.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Horatio scoffs at the Ghost until he sees it, Hamlet doubts the spirit may be a devil and tests it, and he doubts everyone's honesty, from Ophelia to his schoolfellows.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Hamlet gropes for the start of the Pyrrhus speech, and Polonius loses his thread with Reynaldo and asks what he was about to say.

confused.why: The court cannot fathom Hamlet's antic disposition, Polonius guesses wrong, Ophelia's songs confuse all who hear them, and Hamlet himself cannot settle what the Ghost is.

frustrated.why: Hamlet rails at his own inaction, Claudius finds Hamlet alive after the England plot fails, and Laertes' poisoned foil misses its first mark.

uncertain-certain.why: Whether to be or not to be, whether the Ghost is honest, whether to strike Claudius at prayer: Hamlet's indecision is the play's engine.

understanding.why: By the last act Hamlet has understood that there is a divinity that shapes our ends and that the readiness is all.

inspired.why: The play's the thing: Hamlet hits on the Mousetrap to catch the king's conscience, and later on rewriting the commission to doom Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

satisfied.why: Hamlet is satisfied that the Mousetrap proved the Ghost's word, and at the end the revenge is done, though it costs every life.

foreboding.why: Horatio recalls the omens before Caesar's fall, something is rotten in the state of Denmark, and Hamlet feels how ill all is about his heart before the duel.

nostalgia.why: Hamlet holds Yorick's skull and recalls riding on his back and his jests, and looks back to a father who was Hyperion and a mother who hung on him.

anticipation-suspense.why: Horatio and Hamlet wait for the Ghost at midnight, Hamlet watches Claudius's face during the play, and the fencing match is rigged on both sides.

hope.why: Gertrude hopes Ophelia's good beauties are the cause of Hamlet's wildness and may restore him, and Claudius hopes England will cure his fever.

schadenfreude.why: Hamlet relishes having the engineer hoist with his own petard, gloats over Claudius's panic at the play, and feels no pang for Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

elevation.why: Laertes and Hamlet exchange forgiveness as they die, and Horatio's wish to follow his prince is a moment of moral beauty.

infatuation.why: Hamlet's letters call Ophelia his soul's idol, and Polonius diagnoses Hamlet's madness as the ecstasy of love.

rage.why: Laertes storms the palace crying to hell with allegiance, and Hamlet, in a towering passion, grapples with him in Ophelia's grave.
